explanations.explanation: An alliance is right, baker. The LORD says they form one, but against His will, heaping up sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). A plan can look smart on paper and still not be His. And these folks heaped up their sin like I heap chocolate chips on a batch, which is WAY too many.

The LORD never mentions a new army here. He says they form an alliance, but against His will (Isaiah 30:1). An alliance means teaming up with somebody else, and the very next verse says who. I get why an army came to mind, since those two like to show up together.

No royal council in this verse, friend. The LORD says they form an alliance, but against His will (Isaiah 30:1). That's a deal with someone outside their own walls, and verse 2 names Pharaoh, Egypt's king. A council sounds fancy, I'll give you that. I'd put one on my own door if I could.

The LORD doesn't call it a small slip. He says they are heaping up sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). Heaping means it's piling up, one thing on top of another. He starts with “Woe,” and nobody opens with that over a tiny mistake.

That's right, baker. The LORD begins with “Woe to the rebellious children,” and says they are heaping up sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). That's a pile, not a slip. A slip is when I drop one cookie on the floor, and this is a lot bigger than that.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says they set out to go down to Egypt without asking His advice (Isaiah 30:2). They made the plan and headed out without Him. It's like starting a road trip and never once looking at the map.

Right. The LORD says they set out for Egypt without asking His advice (Isaiah 30:2). They went to seek shelter under Pharaoh's protection, and they never checked in with Him first. That's a big thing to skip.

Shame is the word, baker. The LORD says Pharaoh's protection will become their shame, and the refuge of Egypt's shade their disgrace (Isaiah 30:3). They went looking for shelter and got the opposite. I'd want my money back.

Strength sounds like what they were hoping for, I bet. But the LORD says Pharaoh's protection will become their shame (Isaiah 30:3). The shade they were running to turns into disgrace. They wanted a roof and got a lecture.

A fortress would be nice, friend. But the LORD says Pharaoh's protection will become their shame, and the refuge of Egypt's shade their disgrace (Isaiah 30:3). Nothing in that verse turns into a fortress. What they were counting on gives them shame instead.

Yes, baker. The LORD says they bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace (Isaiah 30:5). The people of Egypt are called a people useless to them. That's a whole trip made for nothing, with no help and no benefit at the end of it.

No soldiers in this verse, friend. The LORD says the Egyptians bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace (Isaiah 30:5). If a soldier was coming, it would have been help. And help is exactly what He says they don't bring.

The gold actually moves the other way. In the next verse, they carry their wealth and treasures to a people of no profit to them (Isaiah 30:6). The LORD says Egypt brings neither help nor benefit (Isaiah 30:5). So the treasury isn't getting any gold out of this deal.

That's it, baker. They carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). So the treasure is loaded up and walking right through lions and vipers. That's a lot of risk for a people of no profit to them.

The verse has no ships and no Nile. It says they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). This trip is through a land of hardship and distress. It's all on foot, with animals doing the hauling.

No carts and no oxen here, friend. The verse says they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). It's all loaded on the animals themselves. That's one wobbly way to move treasure past lions.

Rahab Who Sits Still, yes. The LORD says Egypt's help is futile and empty, therefore He has called her that (Isaiah 30:7). So the name here belongs to Egypt. And the name says it all: all that reputation and she just sits there.

That's a mighty name, but it isn't the one in this verse. The LORD says Egypt's help is futile and empty, therefore He has called her Rahab Who Sits Still (Isaiah 30:7). The name tells you what her help does, which is nothing. Sitting still isn't much of a rescue.

That name doesn't show up in this verse, baker. The LORD says Egypt's help is futile and empty, therefore He has called her Rahab Who Sits Still (Isaiah 30:7). It's not a scary name. It's a name about help that never gets up to help.

It reaches a lot further than one day. The LORD says it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever (Isaiah 30:8). He tells Isaiah to write it on a tablet and inscribe it on a scroll. That's a message meant to last.

Right, baker. The writing is for the days to come, a witness forever and ever (Isaiah 30:8). It's put on a tablet and a scroll so it can be read later. Nobody carves something in stone for just one afternoon.

Pleasant is the word. They tell the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.” (Isaiah 30:10). They asked for nice words in place of true ones. That's like asking me to say every cookie is perfect, including the one shaped like a puddle.

It's the opposite, friend. They tell the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.” (Isaiah 30:10). They wanted soft words, not hard ones. And they asked for illusions in place of the truth.
Ancient isn't the word they ask for, baker. They say, “Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.” (Isaiah 30:10). They didn't care how old the words were. They cared how nice they sounded.

True, baker. They say, “Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!” (Isaiah 30:11). That's a name for God, and they want Him gone from their path. It's a hard thing to read.
It is true, friend, and it's a hard verse. The people say, “Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!” (Isaiah 30:11). That's a name for God. They're asking the prophets to get Him out of their way.

That's it, baker. The text says the collapse of that bulging wall will come suddenly, in an instant (Isaiah 30:13). There's no slow creeping about it. One moment it's standing there, and the next moment it's down.
It's the opposite, friend. The wall's collapse will come suddenly, in an instant (Isaiah 30:13). Nothing in the verse mentions years of waiting. It all happens at once.

The verse doesn't say anything about a long warning. It says the collapse of the wall will come suddenly, in an instant (Isaiah 30:13). That's the whole picture it gives. Nobody gets to say, 'Hold on, let me move my stuff.'

True, baker. Not a shard will be found in the dust large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth or to skim the water from a cistern (Isaiah 30:14). It breaks like a potter's jar, shattered. Not one piece is big enough for a job.

It's true, friend. The jar is shattered so that no fragment can be found, and not a shard will be large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth (Isaiah 30:14). A broken cookie can still be eaten. This jar is broken past that.

Repentance and rest, yes. The Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence” (Isaiah 30:15). That's a very different plan from the one they made. It asks them to turn back and be still.

That's more like the plan they already made, baker. They loaded up treasure and went to Egypt, and it didn't help them (Isaiah 30:5-6). The Lord GOD says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved” (Isaiah 30:15). It's a plan with no gifts in it.

No walls or weapons are mentioned here, friend. The Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence” (Isaiah 30:15). It's a quiet way. No building or gearing up, just turning back and resting.
It's the other way around, baker. The Lord GOD offers repentance, rest and quiet confidence, “but you were not willing” (Isaiah 30:15). The way was open to them. They just wouldn't take it.

Right, friend. The Lord GOD says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence—but you were not willing.” (Isaiah 30:15). The offer was there, and they weren't willing. That's heavy, and I think it's a sad line.

Faster is right, baker. The people say, “We will ride swift horses,” but the text says their pursuers will be faster (Isaiah 30:16). Their swift horses don't win the race. Whoever's chasing them has the speed advantage.

That would be good news for the horses, but it isn't what the text says. The people say, “We will ride swift horses,” but their pursuers will be faster (Isaiah 30:16). Their plan to outrun trouble doesn't work. I'd have loved a slower pursuer for my own cookie sheet chasing days, but no.

Weary isn't the word in this verse, friend. The text says that even if they ride swift horses, their pursuers will be faster (Isaiah 30:16). Nobody gets tired in the way they hoped. The ones chasing them are just quicker.
Just one, baker. A thousand will flee at the threat of one (Isaiah 30:17). That's a thousand people running from a single threat. Hard to picture, and a little funny if it weren't so sad.
The number goes the other direction, friend. A thousand will flee at the threat of one (Isaiah 30:17). Only one is doing the threatening. It's a huge crowd running from a very small number.
No army is needed in this verse, baker. A thousand will flee at the threat of one (Isaiah 30:17). That's one threat, and a thousand people take off running. Not much of an army, and still it works.

Alone is the word, baker. At the threat of five you will all flee, until you are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill (Isaiah 30:17). A pole or a banner stands by itself up there. It's a lonely picture.

Safe sounds nice, friend, but it isn't there. The text says they flee until they are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill (Isaiah 30:17). Nothing in the verse says they get to safety. They end up on their own.

Hidden is the opposite of the picture, baker. They're left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill (Isaiah 30:17). A pole on a mountaintop sticks out where everybody can see it. There's nowhere to duck behind.
